label: Heme / Onc
blurb: Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, chemotherapy, targeted and immune therapy

drugs.name: Unfractionated Heparin
drugs.primaryEffect: Immediate anticoagulation with a short half-life
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acute venous thromboembolism, acute coronary syndrome, bridging anticoagulation, anticoagulation during dialysis and cardiopulmonary bypass
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds antithrombin III and induces a conformational change that accelerates its inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa by roughly one thousand fold.
drugs.sideEffects: Bleeding, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with paradoxical thrombosis, osteoporosis with prolonged use, hyperkalemia from aldosterone suppression
drugs.contraindications: Active major bleeding, history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, severe thrombocytopenia, recent neuraxial procedure
drugs.tooltip: Monitored with aPTT and reversed by protamine sulfate. Preferred in renal failure and when rapid reversal may be needed, since its effect disappears within hours of stopping.

drugs.name: Enoxaparin
drugs.primaryEffect: Predictable anticoagulation without routine monitoring
drugs.treatmentUsage: Venous thromboembolism treatment and prophylaxis, acute coronary syndrome, anticoagulation in pregnancy and malignancy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds antithrombin III but its shorter chains preferentially accelerate inactivation of factor Xa over thrombin, giving a predictable dose-response relationship.
drugs.sideEffects: Bleeding, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (less common than unfractionated), spinal hematoma with neuraxial anesthesia, hyperkalemia, osteoporosis
drugs.contraindications: Active bleeding, history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, creatinine clearance below 30 without dose adjustment, recent neuraxial procedure
drugs.tooltip: The anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta, and in cancer-associated thrombosis. Monitored with anti-Xa levels if needed, and only partially reversed by protamine.

drugs.name: Warfarin
drugs.primaryEffect: Delayed but sustained anticoagulation
drugs.treatmentUsage: Mechanical heart valves, atrial fibrillation with valvular disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, venous thromboembolism
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing regeneration of reduced vitamin K needed for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S.
drugs.sideEffects: Bleeding, warfarin-induced skin necrosis in protein C deficiency, teratogenicity with fetal warfarin syndrome, purple toe syndrome, extensive drug and dietary interactions
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, active bleeding, severe hepatic disease, noncompliance with monitoring, recent neurosurgery
drugs.tooltip: Protein C has the shortest half-life, so early warfarin creates a transient hypercoagulable state — hence bridging with heparin and the risk of skin necrosis. Reversed with vitamin K and 4-factor PCC.

drugs.name: Apixaban
drugs.primaryEffect: Predictable anticoagulation without monitoring
drugs.treatmentUsage: Nonvalvular atrial fibrillation stroke prevention, venous thromboembolism treatment and prophylaxis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Directly and reversibly binds the active site of factor Xa, inhibiting both free and clot-bound Xa without requiring antithrombin as a cofactor.
drugs.sideEffects: Bleeding (less intracranial hemorrhage than warfarin), anemia, nausea, spinal hematoma with neuraxial anesthesia
drugs.contraindications: Mechanical heart valves, moderate to severe mitral stenosis, antiphospholipid syndrome, active bleeding, severe hepatic impairment
drugs.tooltip: Direct oral anticoagulants must not be used for mechanical valves or antiphospholipid syndrome, where warfarin remains superior. Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent.

drugs.name: Dabigatran
drugs.primaryEffect: Direct inhibition of thrombin with a specific reversal agent
drugs.treatmentUsage: Nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism treatment and prophylaxis after hip replacement
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Reversibly and directly binds the active site of thrombin, blocking conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin and thrombin-mediated platelet activation.
drugs.sideEffects: Dyspepsia and gastritis, gastrointestinal bleeding more than warfarin, bleeding, spinal hematoma
drugs.contraindications: Mechanical heart valves, creatinine clearance below 30, active bleeding, concurrent strong P-glycoprotein inducers such as rifampin
drugs.tooltip: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that reverses it within minutes, which was the first specific DOAC antidote. Heavily renally cleared, so kidney function limits its use.

drugs.name: Aspirin
drugs.primaryEffect: Irreversibly inhibits platelet aggregation for the platelet lifespan
drugs.treatmentUsage: Secondary prevention of myocardial infarction and stroke, acute coronary syndrome, preeclampsia prevention, colorectal cancer chemoprevention
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase-1 in platelets, blocking thromboxane A2 synthesis; because platelets lack nuclei they cannot regenerate the enzyme for their 7 to 10 day lifespan.
drugs.sideEffects: Gastrointestinal bleeding and ulceration, tinnitus at high doses, Reye syndrome in children with viral illness, bronchospasm in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, hyperuricemia at low doses
drugs.contraindications: Children with viral infection, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, active peptic ulcer, third trimester of pregnancy, bleeding disorders
drugs.tooltip: The irreversibility is the key concept: effects last the full platelet lifespan, so aspirin is held 7 days before surgery. Reye syndrome makes it contraindicated in febrile children.

drugs.name: Clopidogrel
drugs.primaryEffect: Irreversibly blocks ADP-mediated platelet activation
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acute coronary syndrome, after coronary stent placement, secondary stroke prevention, peripheral arterial disease
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A prodrug activated by CYP2C19 whose metabolite irreversibly binds the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor, preventing ADP-induced activation of the GPIIb/IIIa complex.
drugs.sideEffects: Bleeding, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura rarely, rash, diarrhea, neutropenia
drugs.contraindications: Active bleeding, CYP2C19 poor metabolizer status reduces efficacy (boxed warning), concurrent omeprazole
drugs.tooltip: Requires CYP2C19 activation, so poor metabolizers and patients on omeprazole get inadequate platelet inhibition. Prasugrel and ticagrelor do not have this limitation.

drugs.name: Ticagrelor
drugs.primaryEffect: Reversible and more potent platelet inhibition
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acute coronary syndrome including after percutaneous coronary intervention, high-risk coronary artery disease
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Reversibly and allosterically inhibits the P2Y12 receptor without requiring metabolic activation, providing faster onset and greater platelet inhibition than clopidogrel.
drugs.sideEffects: Dyspnea from adenosine accumulation, bleeding, ventricular pauses and bradycardia, elevated uric acid and creatinine
drugs.contraindications: Active bleeding, history of intracranial hemorrhage, severe hepatic impairment, aspirin doses above 100 mg daily which reduce its benefit
drugs.tooltip: The dyspnea affects up to 15 percent of patients and comes from inhibited adenosine reuptake, not cardiac or pulmonary disease. Its reversibility means a shorter washout before surgery.

drugs.name: Alteplase
drugs.primaryEffect: Enzymatically dissolves formed thrombus
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acute ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours, massive pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic instability, ST-elevation myocardial infarction when PCI is unavailable, occluded catheters
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Recombinant tissue plasminogen activator that binds fibrin and converts fibrin-bound plasminogen into plasmin, which cleaves the fibrin mesh holding the clot together.
drugs.sideEffects: Intracranial hemorrhage, systemic bleeding, angioedema, reperfusion arrhythmias, hypotension
drugs.contraindications: Active internal bleeding, prior intracranial hemorrhage, recent stroke or major surgery, blood pressure above 185/110, platelets below 100,000, known aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation
drugs.tooltip: Fibrin-specific, unlike streptokinase, which reduces systemic fibrinogen depletion. Antithrombotics are withheld for 24 hours after stroke thrombolysis to limit hemorrhagic transformation.

drugs.name: Protamine Sulfate
drugs.primaryEffect: Neutralizes heparin anticoagulation
drugs.treatmentUsage: Heparin overdose with bleeding, reversal after cardiopulmonary bypass, partial reversal of low molecular weight heparin
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A highly positively charged protein that binds ionically to negatively charged heparin, forming an inactive complex that is cleared from circulation.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypotension, bradycardia, anaphylaxis especially in patients with fish allergy or prior protamine-containing insulin exposure, pulmonary hypertension, paradoxical anticoagulation in excess
drugs.contraindications: Prior severe protamine reaction; caution in fish allergy, vasectomy, and prior NPH insulin use
drugs.tooltip: Only partially reverses low molecular weight heparin (about 60 percent) and does not reverse fondaparinux at all. Excess protamine is itself a weak anticoagulant.

drugs.name: Vitamin K (Phytonadione)
drugs.primaryEffect: Restores synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors
drugs.treatmentUsage: Warfarin reversal, vitamin K deficiency bleeding of the newborn, malabsorption-related coagulopathy, cholestatic liver disease
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Provides the substrate for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase to carboxylate factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S, restoring their calcium-binding and coagulant function.
drugs.sideEffects: Anaphylactoid reactions with rapid intravenous administration, flushing, warfarin resistance for days after high doses, injection site pain
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; intravenous doses must be infused slowly because of anaphylactoid risk
drugs.tooltip: Onset takes 6 to 24 hours because new factors must be synthesized, so life-threatening bleeding requires 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate for immediate correction.

drugs.name: Ferrous Sulfate
drugs.primaryEffect: Replenishes iron stores and corrects anemia
drugs.treatmentUsage: Iron deficiency anemia, iron deficiency without anemia, pregnancy supplementation
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Provides ferrous iron absorbed in the duodenum by the divalent metal transporter, replenishing stores for incorporation into hemoglobin during erythropoiesis.
drugs.sideEffects: Constipation, nausea, epigastric pain, black stools, tooth staining with liquid forms, severe toxicity in pediatric overdose
drugs.contraindications: Hemochromatosis, hemosiderosis, anemia not caused by iron deficiency, active peptic ulcer relative
drugs.tooltip: Alternate-day dosing improves absorption because a daily dose raises hepcidin and blocks the next day's uptake. Vitamin C enhances absorption; PPIs, calcium, and tea inhibit it.

drugs.name: Deferoxamine
drugs.primaryEffect: Binds and removes excess iron from the body
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acute iron poisoning, transfusional iron overload in thalassemia and sickle cell disease, hemochromatosis when phlebotomy is not possible
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A siderophore that chelates free ferric iron with very high affinity, forming ferrioxamine which is excreted in urine and gives it a reddish color.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypotension with rapid infusion, reddish urine, ototoxicity and retinal toxicity with prolonged use, growth retardation in children, Yersinia and Mucor infections
drugs.contraindications: Severe renal disease or anuria unless dialysis is available; hypersensitivity
drugs.tooltip: Yersinia enterocolitica and Mucor use siderophores, so chelation therapy paradoxically increases their virulence — a memorable exam association. Deferasirox is the oral alternative.

drugs.name: Hydroxyurea
drugs.primaryEffect: Increases fetal hemoglobin and reduces sickling
drugs.treatmentUsage: Sickle cell disease to reduce pain crises and acute chest syndrome, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, chronic myeloid leukemia cytoreduction
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, blocking conversion of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides and arresting cells in S phase; it also induces fetal hemoglobin production.
drugs.sideEffects: Myelosuppression, megaloblastic changes, skin ulceration especially of the legs, hyperpigmentation, secondary leukemia risk, teratogenicity
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, severe myelosuppression, severe anemia; requires regular blood count monitoring
drugs.tooltip: Fetal hemoglobin does not participate in HbS polymerization, so raising HbF directly reduces sickling. It is the only disease-modifying drug proven to reduce mortality in sickle cell disease.

drugs.name: Methotrexate
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks folate-dependent DNA and RNA synthesis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia, lymphoma, osteosarcoma, choriocarcinoma, ectopic pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting tetrahydrofolate needed for thymidylate and purine synthesis, thereby halting DNA replication in S phase.
drugs.sideEffects: Myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, pulmonary fibrosis, nephrotoxicity at high dose, macrovesicular steatosis, teratogenicity
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, significant renal or hepatic impairment, active infection, pleural effusion or ascites which act as drug reservoirs, concurrent trimethoprim
drugs.tooltip: Leucovorin rescue supplies reduced folate downstream of the enzymatic block, sparing normal cells. Weekly, not daily, dosing in rheumatology — daily dosing errors have been fatal.

drugs.name: 5-Fluorouracil
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks thymidine synthesis and DNA replication
drugs.treatmentUsage: Colorectal, gastric, pancreatic, and breast cancer; topical treatment of actinic keratosis and basal cell carcinoma
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Converted to 5-FdUMP, which forms a covalent ternary complex with thymidylate synthase and folate, irreversibly blocking synthesis of thymidine and causing thymineless cell death.
drugs.sideEffects: Myelosuppression, mucositis and diarrhea, hand-foot syndrome, coronary vasospasm, photosensitivity, severe toxicity in dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency
drugs.contraindications: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency, pregnancy, severe myelosuppression, poor nutritional status
drugs.tooltip: Leucovorin paradoxically enhances 5-FU by stabilizing the ternary complex, the opposite of its rescue role with methotrexate. Screen for DPD deficiency, which causes life-threatening toxicity.

drugs.name: Cisplatin
drugs.primaryEffect: Cross-links DNA and triggers apoptosis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Testicular, ovarian, bladder, lung, head and neck cancers
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Forms intrastrand and interstrand platinum-DNA cross-links, primarily at guanine N7 positions, distorting the double helix and blocking replication and transcription.
drugs.sideEffects: Nephrotoxicity with magnesium wasting, irreversible ototoxicity, severe nausea and vomiting, peripheral neuropathy, myelosuppression
drugs.contraindications: Preexisting renal impairment, hearing loss, prior severe reaction; requires aggressive hydration and often amifostine
drugs.tooltip: Aggressive saline hydration with magnesium repletion is mandatory to protect the kidneys. Amifostine is a free radical scavenger given specifically to reduce cisplatin nephrotoxicity.

drugs.name: Cyclophosphamide
drugs.primaryEffect: Cross-links DNA in rapidly dividing cells
drugs.treatmentUsage: Lymphoma, leukemia, breast cancer, sarcoma, lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis, conditioning before stem cell transplant
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A prodrug hepatically activated to phosphoramide mustard, which alkylates and cross-links DNA at guanine N7, and to acrolein, which is responsible for bladder toxicity.
drugs.sideEffects: Hemorrhagic cystitis and bladder cancer, myelosuppression, SIADH, infertility, secondary malignancy, alopecia, nausea
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, severe bone marrow suppression, urinary outflow obstruction, active severe infection
drugs.tooltip: Mesna binds acrolein in the urine and is co-administered with aggressive hydration to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis. Acrolein has no antitumor activity — it is pure toxicity.

drugs.name: Doxorubicin
drugs.primaryEffect: Intercalates DNA and generates free radicals
drugs.treatmentUsage: Breast cancer, lymphoma, leukemia, sarcoma, and many solid tumors
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Intercalates between DNA base pairs, inhibits topoisomerase II causing double-strand breaks, and generates iron-dependent free radicals that damage DNA and membranes.
drugs.sideEffects: Dose-dependent irreversible dilated cardiomyopathy, myelosuppression, alopecia, severe vesicant tissue necrosis with extravasation, red urine, secondary leukemia
drugs.contraindications: Baseline ejection fraction below 50 percent, cumulative dose above roughly 550 mg/m2, severe hepatic impairment
drugs.tooltip: Cardiotoxicity is cumulative-dose dependent and largely irreversible; echocardiograms track ejection fraction. Dexrazoxane is an iron-chelating cardioprotectant that reduces free radical damage.

drugs.name: Bleomycin
drugs.primaryEffect: Induces DNA strand breaks without myelosuppression
drugs.treatmentUsage: Testicular cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, pleurodesis for malignant effusion
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Forms a complex with iron and oxygen that generates free radicals causing single and double-strand DNA breaks, acting mainly in the G2 phase.
drugs.sideEffects: Pulmonary fibrosis (dose-limiting and sometimes fatal), skin hyperpigmentation, Raynaud phenomenon, fever and chills, minimal myelosuppression
drugs.contraindications: Preexisting significant pulmonary disease; high inspired oxygen concentrations dramatically accelerate lung injury
drugs.tooltip: The classic pairing on exams: bleomycin and pulmonary fibrosis. Anesthesiologists deliberately limit FiO2 in these patients because oxygen fuels the free radical lung injury.

drugs.name: Vincristine
drugs.primaryEffect: Arrests mitosis by preventing spindle formation
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Wilms tumor, neuroblastoma
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds beta-tubulin and prevents microtubule polymerization, so the mitotic spindle cannot assemble and cells arrest in metaphase.
drugs.sideEffects: Peripheral neuropathy that is dose-limiting, constipation and paralytic ileus, SIADH, vesicant tissue necrosis, minimal myelosuppression
drugs.contraindications: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and other hereditary neuropathies; fatal if given intrathecally (must always be labeled for intravenous use only)
drugs.tooltip: Intrathecal administration is uniformly fatal, one of the most serious medication errors in oncology. Vincristine spares marrow but causes neuropathy; vinblastine does the reverse.

drugs.name: Paclitaxel
drugs.primaryEffect: Freezes microtubules and blocks mitosis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Breast, ovarian, lung, and esophageal cancer; drug-eluting coronary stents
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Hyperstabilizes polymerized microtubules by binding beta-tubulin, preventing the depolymerization required for the spindle to separate chromosomes in anaphase.
drugs.sideEffects: Peripheral neuropathy, myelosuppression, hypersensitivity to the cremophor vehicle requiring premedication, alopecia, bradycardia, myalgias
drugs.contraindications: Neutrophil count below 1500, prior severe hypersensitivity, significant preexisting neuropathy
drugs.tooltip: The mirror image of vinca alkaloids: taxanes stabilize microtubules so they cannot break down, while vincas prevent them from forming. Both arrest mitosis.

drugs.name: Imatinib
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks constitutively active BCR-ABL kinase
drugs.treatmentUsage: Chronic myeloid leukemia with the Philadelphia chromosome, gastrointestinal stromal tumor with c-KIT mutation, Ph-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Occupies the ATP-binding pocket of the BCR-ABL fusion tyrosine kinase, and also of c-KIT and PDGFR, halting the constitutive proliferative signaling they drive.
drugs.sideEffects: Edema especially periorbital, myalgias and muscle cramps, nausea, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, rash, heart failure rarely
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, severe hepatic impairment; numerous CYP3A4 interactions
drugs.tooltip: The proof of concept for targeted cancer therapy, turning chronic myeloid leukemia from fatal to chronic. Resistance arises from BCR-ABL point mutations such as T315I, which requires ponatinib.

drugs.name: Rituximab
drugs.primaryEffect: Depletes CD20-positive B lymphocytes
drugs.treatmentUsage: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, rheumatoid arthritis, ANCA vasculitis, immune thrombocytopenia, multiple sclerosis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds CD20 on B lymphocytes, triggering complement-dependent cytotoxicity, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, and direct apoptosis; plasma cells are spared since they lack CD20.
drugs.sideEffects: Infusion reactions, hepatitis B reactivation (boxed warning), progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, hypogammaglobulinemia, neutropenia, tumor lysis syndrome
drugs.contraindications: Active hepatitis B infection without prophylaxis, active severe infection; screen hepatitis B serology before every course
drugs.tooltip: Screen for hepatitis B before starting — reactivation causes fulminant hepatitis. Because plasma cells lack CD20, existing antibody titers persist while new B cell responses are abolished.

drugs.name: Trastuzumab
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks HER2-driven tumor growth signaling
drugs.treatmentUsage: HER2-positive breast cancer in adjuvant and metastatic settings, HER2-positive gastric cancer
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the extracellular domain of the HER2 receptor, preventing dimerization and downstream signaling while also recruiting antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
drugs.sideEffects: Cardiomyopathy that is usually reversible, infusion reactions, pulmonary toxicity, embryo-fetal toxicity with oligohydramnios
drugs.contraindications: Baseline ejection fraction below 50 percent, pregnancy, concurrent anthracycline use because cardiotoxicity is synergistic
drugs.tooltip: Unlike anthracycline cardiotoxicity, trastuzumab cardiomyopathy is usually reversible and not dose-dependent. Giving it concurrently with doxorubicin sharply increases risk, so they are sequenced.

drugs.name: Bevacizumab
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks tumor angiogenesis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Colorectal, lung, renal cell, and ovarian cancer; glioblastoma; intravitreal use in wet macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds circulating vascular endothelial growth factor A, preventing it from activating VEGFR on endothelial cells and thereby inhibiting new tumor vessel formation.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypertension, proteinuria, impaired wound healing, gastrointestinal perforation, arterial thromboembolism, hemorrhage, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome
drugs.contraindications: Recent surgery or planned surgery within 28 days, hemoptysis, gastrointestinal perforation history, uncontrolled hypertension
drugs.tooltip: The side effects all follow from blocking VEGF, which endothelium needs for maintenance and repair: hypertension, proteinuria, poor wound healing, bleeding, and perforation.

drugs.name: Pembrolizumab
drugs.primaryEffect: Restores T cell recognition and killing of tumor cells
drugs.treatmentUsage: Melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, head and neck cancer, microsatellite instability-high tumors of any origin, Hodgkin lymphoma
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Monoclonal antibody blocking PD-1 on T cells from engaging PD-L1 on tumor cells, removing the inhibitory brake that tumors exploit to evade immune destruction.
drugs.sideEffects: Immune-related adverse events including colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis, hypophysitis, adrenal insufficiency, type 1 diabetes, and dermatitis
drugs.contraindications: Active autoimmune disease requiring systemic immunosuppression, prior solid organ transplant relative, hypersensitivity
drugs.tooltip: Immune-related adverse events can affect any organ and are treated with corticosteroids, not by simply stopping the drug. Endocrinopathies such as hypothyroidism are often permanent.

drugs.name: Filgrastim
drugs.primaryEffect: Increases neutrophil production and shortens neutropenia
drugs.treatmentUsage: Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia prophylaxis, febrile neutropenia, severe congenital neutropenia, stem cell mobilization before apheresis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Recombinant G-CSF that binds receptors on marrow granulocyte precursors, stimulating their proliferation, differentiation, and release into circulation.
drugs.sideEffects: Bone pain (very common), splenomegaly and rare splenic rupture, acute respiratory distress syndrome, leukocytosis, capillary leak syndrome
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to E. coli-derived proteins; do not give within 24 hours of chemotherapy
drugs.tooltip: Bone pain from marrow expansion is the hallmark side effect and responds to antihistamines or NSAIDs. Pegfilgrastim is the long-acting form given once per chemotherapy cycle.

drugs.name: Eltrombopag
drugs.primaryEffect: Increases platelet production
drugs.treatmentUsage: Chronic immune thrombocytopenia, severe aplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia in chronic hepatitis C before interferon therapy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the transmembrane domain of the thrombopoietin receptor on megakaryocyte precursors, activating JAK-STAT signaling and increasing platelet production.
drugs.sideEffects: Hepatotoxicity, thrombosis, cataracts, marrow reticulin fibrosis, rebound thrombocytopenia on discontinuation
drugs.contraindications: Significant hepatic impairment; must be taken away from polyvalent cations including dairy and antacids which chelate it
drugs.tooltip: It increases production rather than reducing destruction, a different strategy from steroids or IVIG in immune thrombocytopenia. Absorption is blocked by calcium, so timing with meals matters.

drugs.name: Romiplostim
drugs.primaryEffect: Stimulates megakaryocyte proliferation and platelet output
drugs.treatmentUsage: Chronic immune thrombocytopenia refractory to steroids, immunoglobulin, or splenectomy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A peptibody that binds and activates the thrombopoietin receptor at the same site as endogenous TPO, triggering JAK2 and STAT5 signaling in megakaryocytes.
drugs.sideEffects: Headache, arthralgia, thrombosis, marrow reticulin fibrosis, rebound thrombocytopenia after stopping
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; caution with myelodysplastic syndrome where blast counts may increase
drugs.tooltip: Weekly subcutaneous injection with no oral absorption issues, unlike eltrombopag. Both agents must be tapered carefully because abrupt withdrawal causes platelets to fall below baseline.

drugs.name: Intravenous Immunoglobulin
drugs.primaryEffect: Rapidly raises platelet count and modulates autoimmunity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Immune thrombocytopenia, Kawasaki disease, Guillain-Barre syndrome, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, primary immunodeficiency
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Pooled donor IgG that saturates splenic macrophage Fc receptors, blocking clearance of antibody-coated platelets, and neutralizes autoantibodies and complement.
drugs.sideEffects: Headache and aseptic meningitis, renal failure with sucrose-containing preparations, thrombosis, anaphylaxis in IgA-deficient patients, volume overload, hemolysis
drugs.contraindications: Selective IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies, severe renal impairment, hyperviscosity states
drugs.tooltip: Works within 24 to 48 hours in immune thrombocytopenia, making it the choice for urgent bleeding, but the effect lasts only weeks. IgA-deficient patients can have anaphylaxis to trace IgA.

drugs.name: Tranexamic Acid
drugs.primaryEffect: Stabilizes clot by preventing fibrinolysis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Trauma-associated hemorrhage, postpartum hemorrhage, heavy menstrual bleeding, hereditary angioedema, dental procedures in hemophilia
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A lysine analog that competitively blocks the lysine binding sites on plasminogen, preventing it from binding fibrin and being converted to active plasmin.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea, diarrhea, thrombosis risk, seizures at high doses especially in cardiac surgery, visual disturbances, hypotension with rapid infusion
drugs.contraindications: Active intravascular clotting, subarachnoid hemorrhage relative, acquired defective color vision, history of venous or arterial thrombosis
drugs.tooltip: In trauma it must be given within three hours of injury to reduce mortality — later administration may increase harm. Mechanism is the mirror image of tPA, which promotes plasmin formation.

drugs.name: Argatroban
drugs.primaryEffect: Anticoagulation without any heparin exposure
drugs.treatmentUsage: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with or without thrombosis, anticoagulation during percutaneous coronary intervention in HIT patients
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Directly and reversibly binds the active site of both free and clot-bound thrombin, independent of antithrombin, blocking fibrin formation and platelet activation.
drugs.sideEffects: Bleeding, hypotension, nausea, elevated INR which complicates transition to warfarin
drugs.contraindications: Active major bleeding; requires dose reduction in hepatic impairment since it is hepatically cleared
drugs.tooltip: Hepatically cleared, making it the preferred agent in renal failure, whereas bivalirudin is renally cleared. It falsely elevates the INR, which complicates warfarin bridging in HIT.

drugs.name: Darbepoetin Alfa
drugs.primaryEffect: Long-acting stimulation of red cell production
drugs.treatmentUsage: Anemia of chronic kidney disease, chemotherapy-induced anemia
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A hyperglycosylated erythropoietin analog with a three-fold longer half-life that binds the erythropoietin receptor to stimulate erythroid progenitor proliferation and survival.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypertension, thrombosis and stroke, tumor progression in some cancers, pure red cell aplasia, seizures
drugs.contraindications: Uncontrolled hypertension, hemoglobin above target, pure red cell aplasia from prior ESA use, curative-intent cancer therapy
drugs.tooltip: Dosed every one to three weeks rather than several times weekly. As with epoetin, iron deficiency must be corrected first or the response will be inadequate.

drugs.name: Lenalidomide
drugs.primaryEffect: Modulates immune function and destroys malignant plasma cells
drugs.treatmentUsage: Multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndrome with deletion 5q, mantle cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds cereblon and redirects the E3 ubiquitin ligase complex to degrade the transcription factors Ikaros and Aiolos, killing myeloma cells and activating T and NK cells.
drugs.sideEffects: Myelosuppression, venous thromboembolism requiring prophylaxis, teratogenicity, fatigue, diarrhea, second primary malignancy
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy (absolute, boxed warning), inability to comply with the risk evaluation program; requires thromboprophylaxis
drugs.tooltip: A thalidomide derivative, so the phocomelia teratogenicity persists and access is tightly restricted. Thromboprophylaxis with aspirin or an anticoagulant is mandatory in myeloma regimens.

drugs.name: Bortezomib
drugs.primaryEffect: Causes toxic protein accumulation in plasma cells
drugs.treatmentUsage: Multiple myeloma, mantle cell lymphoma, AL amyloidosis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Reversibly inhibits the 26S proteasome, preventing degradation of ubiquitinated proteins; plasma cells with high immunoglobulin output are exquisitely sensitive to this stress.
drugs.sideEffects: Painful peripheral neuropathy, thrombocytopenia, herpes zoster reactivation requiring prophylaxis, fatigue, gastrointestinal upset
drugs.contraindications: Severe preexisting neuropathy; must never be given intrathecally, which is fatal
drugs.tooltip: Plasma cells depend on the proteasome to clear misfolded immunoglobulin, which is why they die first. Subcutaneous dosing causes far less neuropathy than intravenous, and acyclovir prophylaxis is standard.

drugs.name: Andexanet Alfa
drugs.primaryEffect: Reverses factor Xa inhibitor anticoagulation
drugs.treatmentUsage: Life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding on apixaban or rivaroxaban
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A recombinant catalytically inactive factor Xa decoy that binds and sequesters direct Xa inhibitors, restoring endogenous factor Xa activity.
drugs.sideEffects: Thrombotic events including myocardial infarction and stroke, infusion reactions, antibody formation, rebound anticoagulation after the infusion ends
drugs.contraindications: None absolute in life-threatening bleeding; thrombotic risk must be weighed and anticoagulation resumed when safe
drugs.tooltip: The counterpart to idarucizumab for dabigatran. Rebound anticoagulation occurs after the infusion stops because sequestered drug redistributes, so monitoring must continue.
